newsitem.title: HUNGARY: INTERVIEW-Danubius CEO urges no dividend.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Danubius CEO urges no dividend.

text.p: The board of Danubius Hotels will propose to the company's annual general meeting on April 29 that no dividend be paid on 1996 results, the company's CEO told Reuters on Friday.
"In the invitation to our shareholders to attend the AGM the board suggests there be no dividend," president and CEO Sandor Betegh said.

Betegh said the decision was taken because of financial commitments involved in Danubius's takeover of the Hungaria Szalloda (formerly HungarHotels) hotel group, its increased stake in the Budapest Helia hotel and ongoing refurbishment programmes.
"We bought HungarHotels with a loan, we are making several hotels refurbishments, and we have to pay the remaining part of the Helia acquisition which will be roughly 600 million forints."
Danubius completed 8.125 billion forint purchase of hotel chain Hungaria Szalloda Rt late last year.

The company secured bridging loans covering 80 percent of the purchase price and paid the remaining 20 percent with compensation coupons, which were issued by the last government to victims of fascism and communism and are traded on the Budapest Stock Exchange.
The company used three banks -- K&H, Creditanstalt and the Magyar Kulkereskedelmi Bank -- to secure the loans, one of which has a maturity of one year and the other two of five years.
Danubius also exercised a purchase option to increase its stake in Budapest's four-star Thermal Hotel Helia to 100 percent in the from 73 percent.
A zero dividend was also recommended at last year's AGM, a decision which Betegh said paid off for the comapny's shareholders.

"It was an excellent decision last year not to pay a dividend because the share price has grown much more significantly than the dividend," he said. "Within one year the share price increased almost four times."
Danubius shares rose in 1996 to over 4,000 forints from 1,200 forints and have since risen to a peak of 6,615 on February 12, 1997. On Friday they closed at 5,300, down 100.
"If we pay five percent that makes 400 million forints, which is nothing for the shareholders when you consider what they made on the share price rise last year."
Danubius had 1996 consolidated after-tax profits of 2.1 billion on net sales of 10 billion forints.
Betegh said he expected Danubius to benefit in 1997 from an increase in consumer spending resulting from an expected upturn in Hungary's economy.

He said he also expected the company's spa hotels to benefit from a recent decision by the German government to reduce the number of paid spa holidays for its citizens from one every three years to one every four years.

"The Germans are therefore looking for spas where they get more value for money and that helps us," he said, adding that 80 percent of provincial hotel guests are spa tourists of whom one out of three is German.
